notes: \cpara{Asks, on the reader's behalf, what the recent posts on joy in the merely real have to do with reductionism.}

\cpara{The first answer: a line of retreat, so that taking things apart does not feel like removing the world's magic. ``Unweaves the rainbow'' echoes Keats's ``Unweave a rainbow'' in \textsc{Lamia}, a few lines after the passage that opens ``Joy in the Merely Real.''}

\cpara{The second answer: against ``Hollywood Rationality,'' the view that understanding the rainbow subtracts its beauty. The reply is the thesis of Richard Dawkins's \textsc{Unweaving the Rainbow} (1998), which takes its title from the same poem and argues, in the words of Wikipedia's article on the poem, that science ``reveals, rather than destroys, the true beauty of the natural world.'' The post does not mention the book.}

\cpara{The third answer, which the post calls deeper, is named here and explained later: ``binding yourself to reality.'' The links go to ``Twelve Virtues of Rationality'' and to a post on ``the Way.''}

\cpara{An image from fiction, offered from memory (``IIRC'') and granted not to work: a Truthsayer who detects lies by never lying. The last sentence gives the theme its first plain statement: press yourself against reality ``without flinching away, or sneering down.''}

\cpara{The first example: hope taken from the lottery and put into a job, a school or a business. It restates ``Lotteries: A Waste of Hope'' (13 April 2007); the notes on that post give the research nearest to the claim that such hopes lead to action.}
\cpara{Separates a hard dream from an impossible one: the lottery is not difficult but ``un-actionable,'' since work does not change the odds.}

\cpara{The post's central idea, stated as a metaphor. ``Emotional energy'' is not defined, and the post gives no evidence that feeling withdrawn from one object, the lottery or a magical rainbow, becomes available for another. The advice to redirect feeling depends on that assumption.}
\cpara{Says the idea is not advice to set safe, ``realistic'' goals, and declines to judge any reader's own case.}
\cpara{Restates the idea with the rainbow: one can care about things that turn out not to be magic.}
\cpara{Draws on ``Feeling Rational'' (26 April 2007): emotions that follow from one's best picture of the truth are not irrational.}
\cfact{The line is P. C. Hodgell's, and ``Feeling Rational'' credits it to Hodgell. The second line is the author's own.}
\cpara{States the programme: redirect the emotions attached to bad explanations into beliefs ``as true as we can make them,'' instead of destroying them.}

\cpara{The clearest example, and the easiest case for the idea: the airplane delivers what the potion promised, flight. In the rainbow case the real thing, the physics of light, is a different pleasure from the magic it replaces.}
\cpara{Points back to ``Think Like Reality'' (2 May 2007), which told readers who find quantum physics weird: ``This is your problem, not reality's.''}
\cpara{Applies that rule to feelings: bind them to the lawful universe, which includes Moon landings and the evolution of intelligence and excludes magic ``anywhere, ever.''}
